From Bell's Weekly Messenger, London May 29, 1843. France þÿ Our intelligence from France is destitute of any particular point of þÿinterest. A report was current in Paris that a deputation from St. Dornitigo had arrived, with a proposition to place that republic under the protection of Prance. When we remember the circumstances which resulted in the liberation of Havti from French Dominion, and the long series of unparalleled cruellies to which the Haytians were subjected, we cannot believe that they have any desire to place themselves under the protection of their former masters. A long discussion took place in the Chamber of Deputies on Tuesday respecting the extraordinary supplies required for Algeria. The sum demanded was 28,005,298 lianes; and the effective foree required to maintain this profitable acquisition was stated tobe 75,000 men. After a long discussion, tiie demand Was agreed to, although some discontent was manifested at the continual drain upon the national resources. They look forward, however, to the speedy overthrow of the Begem and the restoration of the ex-queen Christina þÿ THE AFFAIRS OF PORTUGAL. The interruption of the negociations for effecting a commercial treaty with this country, has been followed by a complete stagnation of business in Oporto and the whole of tfie wine districts of Portugal. The bulk of the labouiers thrown out of employment are suffering severely ; many of them, diivento desperation by want, have formed themselves into bands of thieves, and so numetous ate the robberies which they have committed that no one feels himself to bo safe. Several of the churches have been pillaged: and one hand, consisting of about 30 desperadoes, made an attack upon the rota! church of Eapa, which was obliged to be defended by a detachment of soldiers. þÿ Infamous as was tfie design of lire þÿrobbers, says a correspondent, þÿ was it not more infamous than the

administrative policy which has driven the people of the second city in the kingdom to such diie extiemiues ; and the strangled trade of Oporto clutches, with the mad energies of despair, her churches. " Hunger makes a hole in the at the most sacred relies of hearts of people, and plants hatred there. Such is the extent of brittle in Oporto, that curfew law has been proclaimed, and the municipal guard arrest all persons who are not well known as belonging to respectable families, whom they find in the streets after nine þÿo ciock. In the midst of all this suffering, while there are some who see that the only effectual remedy is the conclusion of a treaty on the just and equitable principles advanced by die British government, there are others who are seeking to inflame the public mind agnmst England and everything English, by the most audacious falsehoods : but which, fortunately are associated with such ludicrous bombast, that we can scarcely refrain from smiling at what appears very much like þÿ a tempest in a tea pot." Here is a rich specimen : þÿ þÿ Treaty! there should he none amongst enemies; or, if Portugal treat with England, it should be by the mouth of pieces of artillery. England sought the protection of Portugal (!) in the early part of this century to make her soil a field of battle for the purpose of afterwards inundating it with her chokedup manufacturing produce. It was England, too, that caused the French to invade tiie Lusitanian territory (!). It was the Portu

guese arms that won the victories upon which England plumes herself (!). Brazil was lost to Portugal through a Biitish intrigue. And, finally, our monetary Claims, our dividends and the like, amount to a downright robbery, and Sir John Doylfe, instead of having ins reclamation liquidated in 1840, after years of anxious delay, ought to have been hanged as a spy by the Portuguese þÿgovernment? This þÿ new way of paying old þÿdebts is truly characteristic of the Punic faith of this portion nl the peninsula. Bat t lie less ihose Lusiianian herons say of hanging the better. They would have been hanged lu a man, bv Jnnot or Miguel on the Gaea do Sodre. but for stalwart British assistance. An intelligent individual, writing on the spot, and who seems perfect I v convoisant with ihe position of allairs, says:- þÿ Let England be hut true to herself, and she may dc'y as wed as despise the mean and

barking malice of her grovelling enemies, Hei great and generous deeds will live in history when the h&nds shall have withered into dust which thus record their base ingratitude and shame But it is moie to the purpose to state that England can lorce the tariff convention, upon her own terms, and that force it she most probably Will if it be not voluntarily ceded. Amongt tier powerful agenis are the following: þÿ 1. To withdraw entirely her protection from Portugal, and leave her at the mercy of her rival, .Spain, who very recently evinced her readiness to fall on her, in a quarrel arising from the navigation of the Douro. þÿ 2. To direct the resources of British skill and energy to providing a substitute for port by the careful preparation of ihe excellent red wines of Spain, which, if tended with due appliances, the world cannot surpass, and by developing and improving the hitherto neglected growths of our Ionian Islands þÿ in latitude and climate the same, and unexcelled in all the finer qua! ities of the grape þÿ 3 To confiim and complete the flat of fashion already sent forth, and which high political circles can render omnipotent, against port, Madeira, Lisbon, and all other growihs of this ungrateful country. and consume the wines of Spain and Sicily, and of our own dependence s of Corfu, Zarite, and the C 'sipe þÿ 4. To cut off Portugal completely from Europe, except by tfie slow and toilsome overland communication through Spain and France, bv altering the terms of

our government contract w iih the Peninsular Steam Company, shutting out Oporto and Lisbon fiom the route of their packets, ami substituting for these two ports Bayonne and Santander, by which the Pyrenees and Bis cavan provinces will be opened to the tourist and to the traveller in pursuit of health. Those of our fellow subjects who desire a mild climate may thus find it in the nortfi of Spain or south of France, while those who seek a Warm climate will discover it in Andalusia, a climate incomparably superior to that of Lisbon, whose unceasing high winds are as trying to the invalid as ihe ait of England. The lesident in the Pyrenees or m any part of Andalusia will find more of interest and I ss of filth than in Lisbon, while touching at so important a point as Bavm ne would remunerate the company better than visiting any part of Portugal; ami the weekly communication by post might still he kept op through- Vigo. þÿ 5. The slightest deviation from existing monetary engagements to be made a casus belli. Retaliation is to be deprecated under ordinary circumstances; hut here it w ill have been absolutely forced npon us. þÿ A clear advantage of this arrangement would be the effectual conciliation of Spoilt, by opening all hpr ports, northern and southern, to constant communication with the most active mercantile country in Europe, and transferring to her the passengers and residents. with well lined purses, of whom a latge proportion now fix themselves in þÿPortugal.-

The application of British capital to the improved preparation of her red wines, and the other preferences thus accorded to her over Portugal, would naturally lead to a reduction of the tat iff' ; her wealth, her power, her national prosperity, would inevitably increase, while those of Portugal would as inevitably dwindle bv her side, until the larger country would absorb the smaller, and Portugal would again become a province of Spain, as she was so late as 200 years ago, and as woiild have long since happened in the very nature of things, but for tfie mighty and illrequited protection of þÿEngland.

From Bell's Weekly Messenger, London April 'A, 1841) THE SOCIETY ISLANDS AND THE FRENCH, Wo tjavo. in our Messenger of last week, an account, derived from a French source, of the circumstances which led to the treaty between Queen Pomare ahd Admiral Dupetit Thenars on the part of France, by which treaty the Society Islands are placed under the protection of the latter power. We expressed our doubts of the correctness of the assertion in the French papers, that the conduct of Queen Pomare was perfectly spontaneous, and we mentioned some facts which appeared to us to justify those doubts. "On September 1, the French frigate of war, sixty guns, the Heine Blanche, Admiral A. Dupetit Thouars, arrived at Papeete. For a few days all appeared quiet 011 board, and professions of peace were extensively circulated by the French On the 5th messengers were dispatched to the Queen, who was slaying at Eimeo (daily expecting confinement), as also to the principal chiefs, requesting them to coine to Papeete, that the admiral might pay his respects to them, and inconsequence all understood that his errand was of a friendly character. On the 8th, the principal chiefs arrived and dined on board with the admiral, and, 011 the same day, we had the first intimation that a meeting was to he held between the chiefs and the French. The same evening the Briiish vice consul and the American consui received an official doe umenl from the ships, stating that differences existed between the Tahitian and French governments, which would probably lead to

hostilities, and ali Biitish and American subjects were warned to secure their persons and property. Earlv 011 the following morning, we ascertained from Mure, the chief speaker, that the expected meeting had been anticipated by a secret one held during the night between four principal chiefs and the I1 t ench. At this meeting a document was signed by the lour chiefs. The document was to the effect already stated. " The 9th was a day of painful suspense. The Queen's consent was not vet obtained. The admiral demanded her signature, or 10.000 dollars, for injuries alleged ; if neither signature nor money was yielded in 24 hours, he declared his intention of planting the French flag and firing his guns; thus formally taking the island and making his own conditions. All saw that the islands were virtually taken, and of two evils it was thought best to choose the least. The Queen signed just one hour before the firing was to commence. Proclamations are now issued, of which one clause states, 'That anv person, who shall either in word or deed prejudice the Tahitian people against ished ' A supreme council of three French- the French government, shall be banmen is appointed. Beyond them there is no appeal but to the King of the French."

Commercial Theaty wtTti Brazil. þÿ The Liverpool Titties contains the following: þÿ " We have received news from Rio to the 9ih of February, which is upwards of a fortnight later than any Which has yet appeared either in the London or any other papers. We regret to say that it is very unfavourable. The accounts from Rio state that Mr. Ellis's mission has entirely failed, and that he is making preparations to return to this country almost immediately in her Majesty's ship Malabar. His proposal for a fresh trealy has been rejected by the Brazilian ministers, the terms not being such as they are willing to accept, but they have offered to treat if the English government will reduce the duties on Brazilian sugar and coffee to the same rates as thode on sugar and coffee, the produce of tfie British colonies! Of course Mr. Ellis has no power to negociste on any such terms. It was understood that he was to give up his house on- the 15th of Febrnarv. and to take on his residence at Johnston's Hotel until the M alabar was ready to sail, unless this display of promptitude and decision should shake the decision of the Brazilian government. The Portuguese Treaty. þÿ By private advices from Lisbon we learn that the propositions of the Portuguese government have been rejected by our cabinet as being unsatisfactory. The course which Portugal will now take is not quite clear, although the issue of the dispute may be pretty accurately guessed. If Lord Aberdeen maintain the position which he has taken, the force of events will soon operate in such a manner upon the Portuguese cabinet as to leave it 110 alternative but that of accepting the terms which England has offered to it.

Death of the Duke of Manchester þÿ The noble duke expired on the morning of the 18th inst. at Rome, Mr. and Lady Georgians Baiilie and several members of his family, being with his grace at his dissolution. The late duke was for some years governor of Jamaica and postmaster general. The deceased is succeeded in the family honours and estates by Iris eldest son, Viscount Mandeville.

Death of the Earu of Abergavenny þÿ This venerable nobleman died on monday morning last at Eridge castle, Kent The noble carl had been for some time gradually sinking under the infirmities consequent on his extreme old age, having entered his 89ih year on the 22nd ult. The deceased eari was a knight of the Thistle, being the senior knight of that " most ancient and most noble order," with the exceptions of the Earl of Catheart and the Earl of Aberdeen.

Death of General the Hon. Fir Charles Colville. þÿ This gallant officer expired early on monday morning last at his villa at Hampstead. The deceased general was second and youngest son of John, ninth Jjord Colvilie, and brother of the present peer. He was 111 his 73d year. Fir George Colville was coionel of the 5ih Fusiliers. a Grand Cross of the Bath, and G:C: H. The Knight Commandership of the Bath vacant by the death of Major General Sir John Savage, Royal Marines, will, it is understood, be conferred on Major General G. Prese.ott Wingrove, Royal Marines, who was present with Nelson at the battle of Trafalgar. He has seen upwards of half a century of service, and. whether ashore or afloat, of the utmost distinction. þÿ United Sercice Gazette.

CHINA, ENGLAND, AND RUSSIA. The following extract of a letter from the Russian frontier, and published in the Leipsic Gazelle, will be read with interest; þÿ þÿ R A ussian merchant, from Kiachta, reported that the peace between England and China excited great anxiety in Russia, because it was foreseen that the English would do the Russian trade great injury. This fear is already partly realised. Shortly after the peace considerable cargoes of English goods arrived from the East Indies in the Chinese harbours, and were exchanged for tea, silk, quassia, and other Chinese productions, at low prices, as money is scarce, and the Chinese do not like to part with it. It was also expected that large consignments of English manufactures would be sent direct in the course of a few months after the peace, 'i he consequences of this altered state ol tilings have already proved injurious to the Asiatic trade from Kiachta, which had increased rapidly during the last five years. The merchants at Kiachta now take great precautions in their choice of goods for the Celestial Empire, because they are obliged, in ordei not to sustain the heavy cost ot a back freight, to dispose of them at current prices. The Russian manufactures cannot, either in price or quality þÿ which latter is generally very inferior þÿ compete with the English. Their trade is always exposed to great difficulties, in consequence of the want of roads, and the insecurity of the transit. It. was formeily supported by high profits only, but these arc

now gone. Under the present circumstances, Russian exports to China will be i educed to those sold at the great fare, where no foreign competition is to be feared. The writer was of opinion that the other nations, besides England, had not much to hope from the opening of the Chinese ports, because the English would take away ail profit, and are able to sell at prices in which only the Americans can hope to rival them. þÿ As for the opium trade he does not think it possible to put a stop to it, the use of opium is so general, even amongst the highest classes of society. Since the prohibition the Dutch, Americans, French, and Spaniards, have shared in the trade, Java and the Phillippincs producing a part cf the stock. The smuggl.ng is of a twofold injury to the Chinese government þÿ firstly, by the loss it causes to the custom duties, and, secondly, by the exportation of the precious metals. By a regular trade the Chinese products went in exchange: it is necessary to pay for i tie smuggled articles in ready money. It ought, however, he adds, to be remembered, that the Chinese government places the moral considerations higher than the financial. Europe, where the financial system so often is the leading principle might often do well in following the example of China. It is believed that in a few years not only the importation but also the cultivation of opium will lie permitted. Should the latter be the case, the commercial relations between English East India and China will undergo a gieat change.

From Bell's Weekly Messenger, London June 12, 1813. REPORTED OCCUPATION OF TILE SANDWICH ISLANDS BY THE BlilTIS II. A paragraph appeared in some of the daily papers last week, staling that the above named islands had been conditionally ceded to England, and that Lord G. Paulet, commander of her Majesty's ship Cnrysfort, had taken possession of them iri the name of Queen Victoria. Sir 11. Feel, in answer to a question put by a member in the House ot Commons, denied that such a circumstance had occurred. It wiii he seen, however, by reference to the extracts which we have given from the intelligence brought by the Great Western, that the report is confirmed; Lut no particulars of the circumstances under which the conditional cession of the islands took place have reached this country. In the meantime our Paris contemporaries seized upon the first statement, and without waiting to ascertain whether the next post would confirm or contradict it, gave vent to their feelings of virtuous indignation at the grasping tyranny of England, and her atrocious conduct in violating the rights and liberties of an unoffending race of people. The conduct of our Parisian contemporaries presents a remarkable illustration of the happy obliviousness which often overcomes the memory of individuals whose prejudices are jo powerful that they couid as soon think of attributing generous motives to their political opponents, as of suspecting the honesty and integrity of their own. We, however, cannot forget that our neighbours attempted to play the same game at the Sandwich Islands

which they did (unlortunately with more success) at the Marquesian and the Georgian groups. As the late proceedings have invested the subject with considerable importancei the following notice of the Sandwich group may not be unacceptable to our readers ; " Passing to the north latitude 20 degrees is Qwvhee, or Hawai, 275 nnles in circumference, which, with 10 others, form a group, and so named by Captain Cook in 1774, in honour of the Earl of Sandwich, then at the head of a flairs. They are less sultry than the West Indies, and there are no hurricanes that prevail at certain seasons, as in the Atlantic. The natives, both male and female, are similar to those of Otuheite. a fine race, and extremely industrious and friendly towards the English, who were the first to civil ize them and propagate Christianity among

®Asrsx xratstrisraiaast asesxaasr 93 A'T23. them. The seat of government is at Kenaruric, the Island of Oahu, where are depo- in sited in a magnificent mausoleum the mortal remains of the late King Tamehameha II. and his Queen, who died in Loudon with the measles in 1 823 when on a visit to his late Majesty King George IV , whom they called father, to offer to put the islands under Ids protection. These, as well as nearly all the islands in the Pacific, are mountainous, but most productive in everything required for man. There are numerous springs ot the purest water. Cattle, sheep, pigs, poultry, iish, &c., are plentiful Corn, fruit, and vegetables of every description, cau be grown in abundance, the soil being most piolific. The sugar cane, coffee, coitou, rice, maize, bananas, cocoa tree, the olive, vine, orange, citron, pomegranate, pines, and other fruits, grow spontaneously, ihe mulberry-tree, for the propagation of the silk worm, is very abundant, and wood and gums of different descriptions abundant in these islands, 'itiere are no reptiles nor beasts of prey, as in 8oulh America, Africa, and Asia. The coiai and pearl fisheries, and the sperm whale, are of most importance to the natives, who are very expert in the making of canoes and their different implements, and carry on a great traffic witli t fie adjacent islands. Besides the English settlers, there a great many missionaries here, particularly from the United S'.ates of America, who have erected churches, chapels, schools ot industry and agriculture, and introduced the art of printing,

'itiere are also some Koman Catholic pilosis, who have succeeded in obtaining converts m some of the islands. The aborigines aie now much civilized and generally profess the Chiistiau religion, as their king Tamehameha 111 , who is au enlightened man, calls himself the chief disciple. Tin! f "Mowing extraordinary case is given in a French Paper ; þÿ I lie sitting Gourt of Apnea I in criminal matters. Iield ai Bologna. in lialv, on the 16'h ult , was the scene of an awful and most extraordinary incident, and indeed the whole circumstances of the case are nearlv of the same striking character. Towards the end ot 1811 Signor Antonio Gagnirao, an opulent merchant of Ferrara, disappeared, and after several days seaich was found dead in a forest, having been evidently overcome, and murdered after a desperate struggle. Upon some strong grounds of suspicion, two men, I oeti and licglucci, who had frequently been employed at his house as porters, were arrested, and after a short examination confessed themselves to have been guilty of the crime, but justified themselves bv protesting that they had not acted from any personal animosity, but only as the agents for hire of the deceased sislerin law, Signora Birgando, ihe widow of a rich landowner, and a woman equally remarkable for her beauty and accomplishments, of whom they complained for having paid them very inadequately lor the deed. 1 Ids accusation, at first, could scarcely he believed, from the station and character of the female, bat it acquired a degree ot credibility from circumstances, and particularly from its being known that the deceased had made a w ill some years before, bequeathing the whole of his large property to the children of Sig-

Dora Birgando in case he hunselt should leave no immediate descendants, hut had lately manifested an intention of marrying one of Ins maid servants. Signora Birgando was arrested and brought to trial, together with Toeti and Ruglucei, before the criminal tribunal of Ferrara. Upon the confession of those two men, corroborated by the strong and positive evidence of four other witnesses, the widow Birgando and her two accomplices were condemned to death, after standing a ceilain time exposed, with ropes round iheir necks, on a pillery to be erected in front of the church. Against this sentence the three convicts appealed to the superior Court of Bologna. The full confirmation of the sentence was universally expected ; but that which neither llie zeal nor talents of her counsel though the most eminent men from the bars of Rome, Ferrara, and þÿBologna, could be expected to effect, was brought about by ods of Providence. It i« said that tnariv of the ironmasters are sustaining a loss of from 25s. to 30s. upon every ton of bar iiou now sold at the current rate of the market, namely. 4/ per ton, and that thev are only pre uited I oni "blowing out" a great nianv of their Inriiacrs tiv a desire to keep their workpeople a going. In this state of things, "there is a proposition," the liirmhiohitrn Gazette tells us, "which finds favour widi some of the leading ironmasters, and there is a probability of a meeting being convened at the Universal Hall of Commerce, to take the subject into consideration Mr. Bosh, the engineer, has submitted plans to the shipwreck committee of the House of Commons now silting, for the construction of a harbour of refuge upon the Goodwin Sands, either on account of government, or by a private association of capitalists to be endowed with certain privileges. The leading feature of the plan is the immense consumption of iron which its adoption would »' ccssitate. li is proposed first to commence with half a mile of embankment, and this alone would require for its completion not less than 35.000 tons of iron, which, at 5 1. per ton, would give 15,000/. Should the whole plan bo carried out for the embankment of rather more than 1 1 miles, about 800.000 tons would he consumed, 7000 men would l>e employed weekly for II years, and 4.000 000/. sterling be thrown into the iron trade alone. The cost of a cubic foot of iron and concrete is Is. 4d., being less than half

the. price of slone, and the working of a ton of iron gives employment to five men per week. Each caisson, according to the scale submitted to parliament, would fie 100 feet long, 54 feet high, and 30 (eel at the base, and to diminish one foot in six. It would contain 172,800 cubic feet, and would weigh 1300 tons of iron, when floated off to its destination to form the embankment wall, and would be filled with concrete; each caisson, when complete, weighing upwards of 13,000 tons." Weighty as this project is, we fear 1hat it is somewhat visionary. The Thames Tunnel would sink into insignificance before the blocking out ol the sea from the Goodwin Sands by an iron embankment. But wo live in an age of wonders.

To be, or not to be thai is the question ! To the Editor of the St. Croix Gazette, My dear Sir ! Many of your Subscribers will no doubt read with pleasure those few scraps taken lrorn a speech lately made by O'Connell at the Repeal Association in Dublin, a speech, whose contents are fraught with important intelligence for Ireland, and which is uttered in a style of strong determination, such as O'Connell on no other occasion ever manifested. It appears that Sir R. Peel in an answer to Lord Jocelyn with regard to the agitation now going on in Ireland, amongst other things said, that " if there was no other alternative but Repeal of the Union or Civil War he would consider Civil War preferable." Mr. O'Connell in answer to this says " we are told that some desperate measures are to be taken for the suppression of public opinion upon the question of Repeal, and that tlicy have it in contemplation to bring in a Coercion Bill. They may annihilate the constitution, hut to this 1 pledge myself, they shall have some trouble in doing so þÿ 1 will go to the House of Commons for the purpose of opposing their bill þÿ they may trample me under their leet, hut I will come back to Iieland, knowing that 1 have done my duty, and that then Ireland wii,L no iieus. 1 set them at defiance, unless they place their heel upon the constitution and degrade themselves in the eyes of Europe and the civilized world by the exercise of downright tyranny to crush me. 1 tell Sir R. Peel that he will go

to the full length, if he stirs at all. A tyrant law or nothing we will have, let him take his choice and extinguish in the blood of the Irish people, the last remnant of their liberties. Ft tends may desert me, lues may threaten me, but 1 will never forsake the path that I have proposed to myself. 1 will violate no law, I will outrage no ordinance of man, nor of Heaven, but as long as there remains to me o. e inch of the constitution on which I can plant my footsteps, 1 will find some Archimedean point, whereupon to plant the lever with which I will still uphold the fainting liberties of my country !" (the delivery of this beautiful passage acted like an electric shock upon the assembly.) In one of the American papers it is stated that at a Repeal Meeting held at New York one of the richest merchants of that city pledged himsell to give a thousand dollars and more it needed, to assist the Irish in case of civil war, and one hundred other gentlemen pledged themselves to lurnisli one hundred dollars each, as soon as the British Government drives the Irish people to revolt. The Editor ol the paper makes the following bold remark " The friends of Ireland in America tell you Sir R. Peel you may pass as many Arm Bills as you can drive through a corrupt parliament þÿ you may go on till doom's day transporting men for having in their houses a Salmon Spear or a Pike handle. We tell you that when the people of Ireland want arms, they must and they shall have them ! Things speak for themselves.

The recital of the particulars is sufficient to chill the blood in our veins þÿ Enoch has been for a long time deranged. þÿ His father had built a house, for the purpose of keeping him confined, a few rods fiom his own dwelling. On Monday night, hi- lather hearing a noise in the building where Enoch was confiued, went out to discover its origin. He was followed by his wife. Before he had arrived at the building where Enoch had been confined he met him, Enoch having escaped from his confinement, and had the leg of a bench in his hand þÿ With this he immediately struck his father, and felled him to the earth, and then sprang upon his mother and knocked her down also, and commenced beating them. In the mean time a younger brother of the maniac, having discovered w hat was going on, took down his gun and snapped it three times at Enoch, while he was dealing death-blows upon his prostrate parents. Before the gun could be fired oil', Enoch sprang toward his brother, wrested the gun from his hands, commenced beating him with it, and finally knocked him down, and then commenced choking him. Liverpool, May 18. þÿ A large quamity of oil has been slopped bv the Customs' authori ties here, in order to have it ascertained whether or not fraud has been attempted ill getting it through the Custom house under the name of lard oil We have before called lite attention erf the mercantile community to the large importations of hogs' lard from America, and have remarked on the fine quality of "nil made from this lard ; indeed, we have seen oil manufactured from it in Liverpool, and which may be pronounced of the finest description. So far, then, it became evident that a new article had appeared in the market, for which there must he a large demand, and it was quite evident that the Americans would be enabled to furnish a huge supply. Lately, they have been bringing across an oil made from this lard, but which ought not to have been admitted, inasmuch as it took from our own oil refiners the manufacture of the article. It seems, however, that brother Jonathan has not. been content with his now trade in hogs' lard and lard oil, but has been setting his wits to Work in order to evade our duties by imposing on the Customs a mixture of sperm oil with the new lard oil. The reduced duly ott sperm oil under the new ta rill' is 25/. per ton ; that ori lard oil is a mere ml valorem duty, the oil not having been contemplated, su that tl it were possible bv adulteration and mixture to get sperm oil admitted under the name of lard oil, an immense profit would accrue to the parties making the importation.

The Custom house authorities here have laid hold of a batch of Jonathan's pretended lard oil, and we can state, for the information of the public, that the oil so seized is found to contain about GO per cent, of sperm oii, arid not more than about 41 per cent, of lard, the article under the name of winch it fins been endeavoured to be palmed off. It will thus he seen that if this oil find passed muster, an immense mischief would have accrued to the regular trader in sperm oil, who would be societlv undermined and driven froin the iiiaiket by parties having an unjust advantage over him. The most extreme vigilance is now needed bv theCustoms in the examination of foreign oils: there is no article of more extending use and importance and it is astonishing what an amazing number of new vegetable oils have lately sprung into notice. The Americans will try ail sorts of schemes to get their sperm oils admitted at low duties, and unless they arc properly tested, they will friqoentlv succeed. Already lite duty on sperm oil has been sufficiently reduced, without any connivance at fraud being allowed to ruin uur own legitimate trade in lite article.

From the JSew Y'irk Commercial Advertiser, May 25, 184a Fuom Montevideo. þÿ We have a long letter from a correspondent at Montevideo, dated April 23, from which we extract the following. The part we omit consists priuci. pally of a description of the comet, corresponding so precisely with our observation of it here, and the accounts from all other parts of the world, that we feel no scruple in passing it by. The writer proceeds : þÿ " In relation to the siege, wo are as we have been for the last forty days. The Buenos Avrean army is just outside of the walls, and there is continual fighting on a small scale. 1 was yesterday w ith General or President Oribe, at his quarters. 1 found hitn a very pleasant man, and apparently a perfect gentleman ; but when speaking of the inhabitants of Montevideo, he applied no softer name than infernal savages, and if the place does not fall, as it must unless aid comes from some foreign nation, 1 have no doubt there will be such a scene of blood as the history of America has seldom presented. As a specimen of this war : þÿ " The department of Maldonado lies about one hundred miles to the Eastward of this, and has been in the hands of both parties, alternately, for the last thirty days. At the last accounts it was in the hands of the government of Montevideo, and most of the American vessels were chartered to go there and load with cattle for this port. General Oribe said to me that Maldonado was at this time in his possession, and thai he had sent down orders to shoot every man who had sold any cattle to those vessels, & should conti-

nue to do so until Montevideo was taken. þÿ The owner is shot for selling his property, to be taken to the capital of the government under which he lives ! This is in accordance with the policy of Rosas. " The United States schooner Enterprize, Captain Wilson, has gone to Maldonado to protect American interests. " We have received notice to day ol a blockade of this port, made by the government of Buenos Ayres, to take effect on the 1st of April, against every thing of provision kind. "The British commodore is expecting very important despatches from his Government in relation to the present crisis, and sends up the British Government steamer from this place to Rio, for the purpose of transmitting the despatches with more expedition. This letter goes by her, to he forwarded from that place. 1 do believe, from all 1 can learn, that if the place holds out thirty days longer the British Government will throw its weight with the Montevidcans, and thus secure their independence ; if not, the blood of thousands will cry from the ground for vengeance on Mr. iMandeville, the British minister at Buenos Ayres, who has encouraged the Montevideans to resistance with an assurance of intervention on the pari of England, and now ha ving placed them where they must, to appearances, soon have their throats cut. he very quietly says he has nothing to do in the business " In addition to the irreparable injury which he has done his Countrymen in Montevideo, he has deeply tarnished the honor of
the British crown, and his disgrace bv removal, which I have no doubt will take place, will hut poorly compensate for the injury his pernicious conduct has tnllictod on thousands.

30&1TSX TEaWOTttaifc By the Britannia, which 1 send you by this conveyance, you w ill see that the English citizens represent Mr. Maiideville's conduct as it should he, arid are not disposed to submit to his sullying the honor of their country " All commercial business has ceased for some time in Montevideo, with the exception ol sales tor daily consumption of the city. þÿ Eiour is in demand at about ten Spanish dollars. " The ship Talbot, of New York, sailed two days since for Canton. " The brigs Gen 1'inckney, of Baltimore, and Syren ot Salem, and schooner Diligence, of Salem, have gone to Maldonado foi cattle. The ba i ques Madonna, of Philadelphia, and Express, of Boston, are also cliurteted to go iheio." OMEGA.

Exhibition of the Deaf and Dumb. þÿ Perhaps none of the anniversary meetings of the last week possessed greater interest, or manifested more gratilyiog results ol benevolent effort, than the exhibition ot the deal and dumb, on Thursday, the lith iust., at the Broadway Tabernacle. Long before the appointed hour the house was crowded to its utmost capacity, so tiiat for those who came alter, theie was room neither to sit nor stand. The exercises were opened precisely at 4 o'clock, by an appropriate player fioin Rev. Dr. Cox, after which the audience were favored by a lew remarks from the venerable president of the institution, the Rev. Dr. Milnor, who spoke of its present condition and facilities, and compared it lavoiably with other existing establishments of a similar nalnie. The pupils were then introduced by Mr. Peel, the principal ot the institution. After he had said a lew words in explanation of the plan and object of the exhibition, lie did not, as he had often done on previous occasions, describe the process of instructing t he deaf mute, nor did he appear to think it necessary to subject every class to a rigid examination ; but having selected the youngest, middle and oldest classes, contented himsell with exhibiting these to establish the complete success of the system employed at the institution. The youngest class, which had been under instruction only seven or eight months, were then brought forward, and their performances conducted by their teacher, Mr. Bartlett.

He commenced by making with his hand the letters of the alphabet, which the pupils represented on the slate, in the written character. He then made signs for the names and qualities of objects, which the pupils wrote out on the slate, and so varied and numerous were these, that they could not tail to give pleasing evidence of the pupils having been faithfully taught, and, considering their great deprivation, of possessing no mean powers of mind. They had also become able, during the short tune they had been under instruction, to connect words in sentences, and in a measure to express their ideas in written discourse. In illustration of this, the word " wish" was given to them to incorporate, which thev did with correctness and insjen- D uitv. One ol the little hovs in this class was called upon to give in pantomime a descrip

tion of hunting, shooting, &.c. which, much to the amusement ol the assembly, lie performed wuli tiiat grace and truth to nature »« peculiar to the deal and dumb. The next clasg introduced, having been under instruction two years longer, not only exhibited much higher attainments, but also a greater degree of intelligence. To show how conversation may be carried on by means ol signs, their teacher. Mr. Gary, asked them a few questions, which they all answered by signs in a manner calculated to excite sympathy and admiration. Among other things they weie asked, "Hew did you come to the city!" They replied, " In the cars." "Why did you come (" " To show that the deal and dumb as well as others can he taught!" " Which would you prefer þÿ to be deaf and dumb or blind?" To this they answered that they much pieferred their present lot. They were asked the reason of litis. One replied that try means of sight be thought ne could more readily acquire knowledge. Another, that through sight he derived much pleasure from which he would otherwise be debarred. In wnttng sentences on the slates they also displayed a ready and lively imagination, with a good knowledge of the principles o! language. They were first required to write in ttieir own phraseology ideas communicated to them by naiural signs. In tics exercise the language of each was entirely oiffeient from that of the rest, while the idea was preserved throughout. A sentence was then dictated to 'hem in signs, and in this case there was not the east

variation among them all, either in wotd or thought. The analytical m do of :nst ruction employed in teaching the deaf u.d dun t , was then illustrated. A sentein c w,« giveu to the pupils, and questions were ask' d th( m with respect to its different parts Andeach agency, quality and action, having been specifically inve.siigaieif. they were required io write out the sentence in full. Original sen tences embodying given words, and uescriptious of simple objects, were also written on the slates by the pupils, ail of which were correctly expressed; some of them displaying i o much versatility and humor.

While these were writing, a little bnv was cal'ed upon to describe objects and actions iu pantomime. His signs were very graphic, and afforded much amusement to lite audience, especially in his description oi the operation of shaving, which he represented so naturally that it was dilFicult to believe the little fellow was not actually subjecting him selfio that dclci.'.alle process.

To show the manner in which the mutes are accustomed to read, two little girls connected with this class came forward with a Bible. Ur. Cox selected, as the passage to be read, the last two verses of the xi. chap, of Matthew It appeared that they had a two fold manner of rending. They first read the portion of Scripture, selected, by spelling each word on their fingers; their teacbi r read the same aloud, with ordinary rapidity; but they had finished before him. lie rematked that this was the way in which (hoy usually committed their lessons to memory. The other mode of reading was that of making a sign for each word. This, it wag remarked, required a complete I now ledge of the meaning of the text. With much gracefulness of motion the same passage as before was fgad in this manner aUo.

The succeeding exercises, however, were the most interesting part of the exhibition. The first class, who had been in the institu tion about six years, and were under the particular instruction of the principal, now made their appearance. They were first required to write original sentences, incorporating words proposed to them. This they did with entire correctness, and in a very pretty style. Terms were then given them to define, which called out in some degree their knowledge of facts as well as of words. An incident was related by a gentleman present, which was communicated to the pupils, in signs, and with great promptitude transferred by them to their slates. We copy 1 tie following, without correction, as written by one ofthe female pupils, a young lady of sixteen ' Some time ago, as a man was walking about the border settlement, looking for his cow, he saw a bear coming down the tree. When he saw it, he was very much afraid, and could not run a way from it, for it was so near him. He hastily went behind the tree, and caught it by its fore feet, and held it ail the night. There was a house a little distance from him, and the man screamed Very loud for help, but the persons who lived in that house did not come to his assistance, So the poor man held the bear all night. " In the morning the man who lived in that house, came to him, with an axe, and said to him, 'Good morning Mr. Dobson,' for that was his name. Mr lJuhson said to him. ' Did voil hoar me call vou last night?'

'Yes, i did,' said the man, ' but 1 did not get out of my bed.' " Vs the man was going to kill the bear, Air. Dobson stopped him, and told him to hold it instead of him. and let him kill it The man did so, and Mr. Dobson took his axo and went home The man held the bear all day, and all night, without any body coining to his assistance. The next day Mr. Dobson came, and killed the bear, with the axe. þÿ Thus he showed that he ought to be kind to his neighbors." While the class was writing this story two young ladies of very intelligent mien appeared in a dialogue in the language of signs, which was translated by i\ir. Beet. No s;tokcn or written piece of this nature could produce the effect of this beautiful exhibition. Kverv idea could be almost read in the expression of tfie countenance, while the gracefulness which pervaded each motion added to the scene a peculiar charm. Another division of the same class now took the place of the others at the slntrs. The gentleman already spoken of related to them an anecdote, and asked their opinion in reference to the conduct of the hero. The manner in which they w rote it, and the judgment pronounced, ate shown bv the folf dlownig specimen from one of the \oung ladies: " Some time ago a young man fell in love with a young lady, so that he asked her to L'-eome his companion for life ; hut unfortunately his fond anticipation was cut off. Deep despair now possessed the mind of that unhappy man Of course he determined to commit suicide. So he, standing on the

summit of a precipice from which he intended to throw himself headlong, looked down, and now courage 'forsook him; he became afraid of it. lie stopped and said to himself Should I throw myself down this dreadful precipice, my poor neck would break, and it

He would be vers looiiah to go annul groaning for tbe only reason of his being rejected by a girl." liev. Or Mo \ ulev here took occasion to state his feelings w th regard to the admission inio his church of three or lour pupils of the institution, two of wiioiii were then engaged in writing at the slate. He spoke of the examination to winch they were subjected, and the unequivocal evidence they gave of evan gehcal piety, and beautifully alluded to the present time, as bringing about in another way what our Savior accomplished by miracles, " 1 he deal hour and the dumb speak." liis remarks were both solemn and interesting, and calculated to produce a happy impression. Questions were then proposed to the class by diiieient persons present, to which they gave most satisfactory answers. In repiy to if te question, " What is a Christian?" one of them wrote the following b'-autilul sentence; þÿ " A Christian is one wiu> is the true friend of our Saviour, and when he does wrong he asks God's pardon. He fears sm. He loves to meditate on the goodness of God." liev. Dr. Cox then asked several religious questions of the pupils, which were interpreted to them bv Mr. I'eet. Among c othei things, p ' he asked, " liow did yon obtain a knowledge of the Supreme Being ?" Their reply was

" Fiom the Bible." " Do you not think it possible to obtain a knowledge of llnri thiongh His works ?" The reply was, " It is possible, but to us not probable." They were .also asked individually where they received their first idea of the Supreme Being. In eveiv case they had been in total daikness on the subject till the light of instruction dawned on their souls. Mr l'eet then introduced to the assembly a deal and dumb voung man named G. G. W. Gamage, ihe son ot Gilbert Ash Gamage, Esq., now deceased, . favoiably known as a contributor to the Commercial Advertiser, whose poetical effusions possessed no inconsiderable merit. This young man, he said, would address the audience by signs, to show that thought could as readily be conveyed ihrough that medium as by spokeu language, and that as used by the educated deaf and dumb, the language of signs was not more mimic acting. 'Ihe address was translated in the course of its deliveiy by Mr Gary, one of the professors. who so well pet formed the duty assigned him us to make it almost appear that the mote was hiinsell a speaker, uniting beauty of thought with great eloquence. He has at our request since written out the same as neatly as can be recollected. It is as follows : þÿ ' Ladies and þÿGentlemen 1 am deaf and dumb ; 1 cannot speak to you, but 1 am requested to deliver a short address by signs. I shall occupy but a few moments. " During the present week meetings arc held in this house by various religious and benevolent societies Written reports

arc here read, and speeches are made on this platform in behalf of seamen, Sabbath schools, the tract and Bible cause, temperance and also iri relation to the supply of the destitute in our own land with the preached gospel,

and sending missionaries to China, to Africa and to the islands of the sea. Now we come I to exhibit what has been done by Christian phiianthiopy for the deaf and dumb. In heathen lands the deaf and dumb are left in utter ignorance ; they are entirely neglected. It is only where the light of the Bible shiues that they are cared for, and means provided for their mental and moral improvement. " The Bible Society and the Tract Society may send their publications into all parts of the world; the word of life may be translated into all the written languages of the earthbut the uneducated deat mute that receive no benefit from these printed works. They are of no use to him. " It was supposed, formerly, that the deaf and dumb bad no souls, þÿ that they were senseless beings, like lire brutes that perish, 'i hey were tegatded as monsters; they weie objects of horror to their relatives, and were, in some cases, even put to death. But in the providence of God a way was discovered by winch tliey might be educated, and now, mainly at first bv the efforts of tbe Abbe de I'Epee and the Abbe ISicaid, to whom we owe our special thanks, and whose memory we delight to cherish, institutions for the deaf and dumb aie established in France, Germany, England, the United States and other countries. And the aeaf mute who was once neglected and left in ignorance and degradation, is now instructed, tieated with respect, and elevated in hts social condition to an equality wuh bis more favored fellow men.

" Before 1 was educated, 1 saw the objects of Nature þÿ tbe giass, the trees, tbe sun, the moon and slais of heaven, but 1 knew not whence they came oi who made them. But 1 know that God, ttie Eternal Spirit, without beginning' and without end the Almighty, wis , and liolv God is ihe author of the visible creation- He spake, and these worlds weie created. " Before receiving any instruction I knew that, i had the pow< r of thought, but I knew not that I had a soul distinct from my body. ! saw other persons die, and 1 saw them boned in the eaith, but J did not know that I also should die. Now. 1 know that my soui is immortal, and that my body, though it wiil return to dust, will be taistd again at the last day. The Sandwich Islands þÿ It will be seen by out extracts that the reported cession cl the Sandwich Islands to Great Britain has taken place, and we believed we were correct in our supposition that the article we before published on the subject was penned by an American, for it is described in that cpiarter as being a most high handed, and unjustifiable act on the part of the British Commander. The Honorable Lord George i'aulel, of the Carysfort, it seems required satisfaction lor a series of wrongs done to the representatives of Great Britain, bv the Sandwich Islands Government, and in consequence of a non compliance to the extent required, the King was compelled to cede the Island to the Queen of Great Britain, with the view to abide her þÿMajesty decision s on the question at issue. The American papers add that the l'rench Consul at these Islands, imagining his nation insulted through hint, by Lapt. Lord George Paulet. (in not saluting him when going on board his ship, and subsequently in not asking him below) had sent an express to Admiral Dopier, commanding at the Marquesas group, stating the cession of the Sandwich Islands to the British, and of the indignity which bad been offered his government. The presence of the Admiral, backed by two or three French frigates, was very shortly expected. On the former subject we find the following remarks in the New \ork Albion: þÿ The natives of the Sandwich Islands are incapable of sell government ; hence wo fiequently hear of the interference of the

French þÿ of the undue influence of the missionaries, and of the misdemeanors of foreigners O of all nations. The British Consul, . Mr. Charlton, was ill used, his property seized. and his successor insulted. England could not permit this to pass unredressed, and she, accordingly sent a ship of war to demand that redress. But the King was not able to comply with all the requisitions, and he therefore surrendered his Islands provisionally untill the decision of the British Government be known." þÿ We can only in the meantime wait patiently the progress of the Affair in London. The private letters that have arrived are not to be relied on. Thev are violent in their tone, written probably by interested persons, and are altogether exparte in their statements. We refer our readers to the official letters which are alone t» be relied on in this stage of the þÿaffair.

AUTOMATON LABOR. At the Institution of the Civil Engineers, in London, a short time ago, a paper was read, desciibir g a machine invented y Air. 1 Colton, the Governor of the Bank of Bugland, for weighing sovereigns, and separating the light ones from those of standard wi ight The machine exhibited was matin by Mr. Napier of the York road, Lambeth, and was so dc icate that it detected with precision a variation of a twel'p thousand two hundred and fiftieth part of the w ight of a sovereign. The coins are placed in a tube or h ipper, from whence they are carried on to a small platform which is suspended over a delicately poised heair, to the other end of which is appended the standard of mint weight. On setting the machine at wo'k, a sovereign is placed upon the platform, nnd it it is full weight a small tongue advances and strikes it oil into a till appointed to recti vs
SAITSX. T<nr

< it ; but, if it is light, the pint form sinks ami btings it within the reach ot another tongue at a lower level, which advances at right angles to the former tongue, and pushes the coin into another till : other coins succeed in rapid rotation, so that lire machine can weigh and sort 10,000 sovereigns in six hums; while an expert teller can, at the utmost only wei"h between 8>000 and 4.000 coins by hand scales in the same time, and even then the optic nerve, by incessant straining, becomes fatigued, and errors occur. The various ingenious contrivances of the machine can only be appreciated by careful examination; but it was declared to tie one of the most satisfactory instances of automaton labor, that had been seen for many years within the walls of the institution.

From the New York S-un, July 6, 1843, I.tfe on Tfii; Ocean. þÿ VVe make the following extract from Life on the þÿOcean, þÿ by Oapt. Little. Whilst lying in the harbor of Campeachy, (being compelled in consequence of the shallowness of the water to anchor about two and a half miles from the shore.) he accidentally, whilst on shore, discovered a plot by eighty Spaniards to take his vessel during the night. He thus proceeds : þÿ As soon as I- had made known to the officers and crew the sanguinary plot, which was about to be enacted, the anchor was lifted and our position altered by running half a mile out to seaward. The anchor was then lot go under foot, and the sails lowered down but not turled. The two long nine-pounders were loaded nearly up to their Muzzles with langrage and giape shot, and all the small arms, such as muskets, pistols, cutlasses, <fcc , were mustered on deck. Supposing they would attack us simultaneously ahead and astern, one of the long nines w as run aft and the other forward, with an equal division of the small arms, as well as the boarding pikes among the men. These preparations being made, the lights were all extinguished except two matches, which couid not be seen, and then all hands were summoned to the quarter deck. þÿ Mv þÿlads. said I, þÿ since we have been together in this vessel, we have been called Upon to pass through many perilous scenes, and 1 have never had any reason so far to doubt your firmness and courage. You will probably again be called upon to-night to defend this vessel ; her safety and our lives

depending upon your firmness and good conduct. These cowardly Spaniards suppose they will fall upon us unawares, and thereby we should become easy victims to their treachery. I hope to prove this night that American seamen are not only alert, hut also fully competent to beat off these dastardly marauders, although they may lar exceed us in numbers. 1 expect they will come upon us head and stern, theiefore wo will divide ourselves into parties. Mr. VV., the chief officer, will take the command of die forecastle, and I will look out for the quarter-deck. Let there he no confusion or disorder, and not a shot he fired until orders he given to that effect; after which, you are to load and fire the small arms with all possible rapidity. Should the Spaniards succeed in getting alongside, the boarding pikes and sabres are your best weapons, so use them freely. If tire breeze should spring up, we will slip and

It was a dear starlight night, scarcely a cloud was seen, and to seaward the hoiizorr was well defined lo such a night objects might be distinguished at a long instance, ho sound was heard except the icvei deration of the roaring surf, or ihe skipping of a porpoise which ever and anon disturbed the suilaee of the waters by a deep splash, or (lie faint moans inrough ihe rigging of the expiring sea breeze. Extraordinary ExImiess. VVe have received by extraordinary express our dispatches from India. The mail from Bombay of the 20th of May, brings no remarkable intelligence. It started 10 days before the usual time in consequence ot the approach of the monsoon rendering the navigation difficult from Bombay to Aden. The chief points of intetest are connected with the proceedings of Sir Chatles Ain pier in Scinde. It appears that Nhere Mnhommed. who was defeated at the battle of Folialie on the 24th of March, had got over the river and incited some of the mountaineers of the Belooche tribes to join his standard, and approach to the banks of the Indus to within five or six miles of Hyderabad. Another chief, Ali Alourad, who had joined the Biitish, was no longer to be depended on Sir Charles Napier had given notice to the former to give up his useless resistance, or he would proceed to rout him. The 15th of May was publicly mentioned as the date of the expected battle. Her þÿMajesty s 28th Regiment had left Kurrachee early in May, and were expected to reach Hyderabad before the 15th. 1 he great portion of other troops were concentrated around Hyderabad, will) the exception of one native regiment, which was Stationed on the right bank.
